claim: The rod outer segment (ROS) is the specialized sensory cilium of rod photoreceptor cells.
source: The unique membrane organization of the rod outer segment (ROS), the specialized sensory cilium of rod photoreceptor cells, provides the foundation for phototransduction, the initial step in vision.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: ROS architecture is characterized by a stack of identically shaped and tightly packed membrane disks loaded with the visual receptor rhodopsin.
source: ROS architecture is characterized by a stack of identically shaped and tightly packed membrane disks loaded with the visual receptor rhodopsin.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: A wide range of genetic aberrations compromise ROS ultrastructure, impairing photoreceptor viability and function.
source: A wide range of genetic aberrations have been reported to compromise ROS ultrastructure, impairing photoreceptor viability and function.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior literature.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography performed on native ROS at molecular resolution provides insights into key structural determinants of ROS membrane architecture.
source: Here, cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) performed on native ROS at molecular resolution provides insights into key structural determinants of ROS membrane architecture.
evidence: This is the main methodological claim of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Two previously observed molecular connectors/spacers exist that likely contribute to the nanometer-scale precise stacking of the ROS disks.
source: Our data confirm the existence of two previously observed molecular connectors/spacers which likely contribute to the nanometer-scale precise stacking of the ROS disks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-ET data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The extreme radius of curvature at the disk rims is enforced by a continuous supramolecular assembly composed of peripherin-2 (PRPH2) and rod outer segment membrane protein 1 (ROM1) oligomers.
source: We further provide evidence that the extreme radius of curvature at the disk rims is enforced by a continuous supramolecular assembly composed of peripherin-2 (PRPH2) and rod outer segment membrane protein 1 (ROM1) oligomers.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by cryo-ET data and subvolume averaging.

claim: Rhodopsin is a transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor that resides in the rod outer segment (ROS).
source: Rho is a transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor that resides in a specialized cellular compartment in rods, the rod outer segment (ROS), which contains a stack of hundreds of identically shaped and precisely spaced membrane disks.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Approximately 50% of the ROS disk membrane area is occupied by Rhodopsin.
source: Approximately 50% of the ROS disk membrane area is occupied by Rho (Palczewski, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Palczewski, 2006.

claim: Each ROS disk is composed of two parallel membranes connected at their periphery by a hairpin-like disk rim.
source: Each disk is composed of two parallel membranes connected at their periphery by a hairpin-like disk rim (Sjostrand, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sjostrand, 1953.

claim: The disk membranes are interrupted by one or more clefts called disk incisures, depending on the species.
source: Dependent on the species, the disk membranes are only interrupted by one or more clefts, so-called disk incisures (Makino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Makino et al., 2012.

claim: The light sensitivity of rods relies on the elaborate ROS membrane architecture, which evolved to maximize the surface area of the membranes.
source: The light sensitivity of rods relies on the elaborate ROS membrane architecture, which seemingly evolved to maximize the surface area of the membranes, thereby maximizing the amount of Rho for photon capture (Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pugh and Lamb, 2000.

claim: The ultrastructure of ROS was described decades ago based on conventional transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
source: The ultrastructure of ROS was described decades ago based on conventional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Sjostrand, 1953; ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sjostrand, 1953.

claim: The ROS disk stacks exhibit two key structural features: (i) the close packing of adjacent disks and (ii) the high curvature of the disk rims.
source: The ROS disk stacks exhibit two key structural features: (i) the close packing of adjacent disks and (ii) the high curvature of the disk rims.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Previous studies suggested that disk stacking may be assisted by the continuity of neighboring disk membranes.
source: Previous studies suggested that disk stacking may be assisted by the continuity of neighboring disk membranes (Robertson, 1965), while others suggested the existence of molecular connectors between adjacent disks (Corless and Schneider, 1987; Roof and Heuser, 1982; Usukura and Yamada, 1981), and between disk rims and the plasma membrane (PM) (Goldberg et al., 2016; Nickell et al., 2007; Roof and Heuser, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robertson, 1965 and other studies.

claim: Previous studies suggested the existence of molecular connectors between adjacent disks.
source: Previous studies suggested that disk stacking may be assisted by the continuity of neighboring disk membranes (Robertson, 1965), while others suggested the existence of molecular connectors between adjacent disks (Corless and Schneider, 1987; Roof and Heuser, 1982; Usukura and Yamada, 1981), and between disk rims and the plasma membrane (PM) (Goldberg et al., 2016; Nickell et al., 2007; Roof and Heuser, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corless and Schneider, 1987; Roof and Heuser, 1982; Usukura and Yamada, 1981.

claim: Previous studies suggested the existence of molecular connectors between disk rims and the plasma membrane.
source: Previous studies suggested that disk stacking may be assisted by the continuity of neighboring disk membranes (Robertson, 1965), while others suggested the existence of molecular connectors between adjacent disks (Corless and Schneider, 1987; Roof and Heuser, 1982; Usukura and Yamada, 1981), and between disk rims and the plasma membrane (PM) (Goldberg et al., 2016; Nickell et al., 2007; Roof and Heuser, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 2016; Nickell et al., 2007; Roof and Heuser, 1982.

claim: EM studies of fixed and stained ROS identified a molecular assembly at disk rims referred to as the 'terminal loop complex'.
source: Furthermore, EM studies of fixed and stained ROS identified a molecular assembly at disk rims referred to as the 'terminal loop complex' (Corless et al., 1987), which was proposed to enforce high membrane curvature.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corless et al., 1987.

claim: The 'terminal loop complex' was proposed to enforce high membrane curvature.
source: Furthermore, EM studies of fixed and stained ROS identified a molecular assembly at disk rims referred to as the 'terminal loop complex' (Corless et al., 1987), which was proposed to enforce high membrane curvature.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corless et al., 1987.

claim: The 'terminal loop complex' is composed of a crescentic density located along the disk perimeter inside the disk lumen.
source: This complex is composed of a crescentic density located along the disk perimeter inside the disk lumen, which was observed to be linked by a transmembrane component to densities that connect neighboring disk rims.
evidence: This is based on prior EM studies.

claim: The 'terminal loop complex' appeared to form a 2D lattice.
source: The 'terminal loop complex' appeared to form a 2D lattice.
evidence: This is based on prior EM studies.

claim: Mammalian ROS contain three abundant membrane proteins which localize exclusively to the disk rim: ABCA4, PRPH2, and ROM1.
source: Mammalian ROS contain three abundant membrane proteins which localize exclusively to the disk rim: the rod cell-specific ATP binding cassette transporter ABCA4, which is important for the long-term viability of the retina (Tsybovsky et al., 2013), and the two small transmembrane proteins, peripherin-2 (PRPH2) (Molday et al., 1987) and ROS membrane protein 1 (ROM1) (Bascom et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsybovsky et al., 2013; Molday et al., 1987; Bascom et al., 1992.

claim: ABCA4 is important for the long-term viability of the retina.
source: Mammalian ROS contain three abundant membrane proteins which localize exclusively to the disk rim: the rod cell-specific ATP binding cassette transporter ABCA4, which is important for the long-term viability of the retina (Tsybovsky et al., 2013), and the two small transmembrane proteins, peripherin-2 (PRPH2) (Molday et al., 1987) and ROS membrane protein 1 (ROM1) (Bascom et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tsybovsky et al., 2013.

claim: PRPH2 and ROM1 are homologs.
source: PRPH2 and ROM1 are homologs (Kevany et al., 2013) thought to associate non-covalently via dimers into homo- and hetero-tetramers (Goldberg and Molday, 1996), which form higher oligomers stabilized through disulfide bonds (Loewen and Molday, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kevany et al., 2013.

claim: PRPH2 and ROM1 associate non-covalently via dimers into homo- and hetero-tetramers.
source: PRPH2 and ROM1 are homologs (Kevany et al., 2013) thought to associate non-covalently via dimers into homo- and hetero-tetramers (Goldberg and Molday, 1996), which form higher oligomers stabilized through disulfide bonds (Loewen and Molday, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goldberg and Molday, 1996.

claim: PRPH2 and ROM1 form higher oligomers stabilized through disulfide bonds.
source: PRPH2 and ROM1 are homologs (Kevany et al., 2013) thought to associate non-covalently via dimers into homo- and hetero-tetramers (Goldberg and Molday, 1996), which form higher oligomers stabilized through disulfide bonds (Loewen and Molday, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Loewen and Molday, 2000.

claim: Isolated PRPH2-ROM1 complexes induce membrane curvature when reconstituted into lipid vesicles in vitro.
source: Isolated PRPH2-ROM1 complexes induce membrane curvature when reconstituted into lipid vesicles in vitro (Kevany et al., 2013), and heterologously expressed PRPH2 generates high curvature membranes in cells (Milstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kevany et al., 2013.

claim: Heterologously expressed PRPH2 generates high curvature membranes in cells.
source: Isolated PRPH2-ROM1 complexes induce membrane curvature when reconstituted into lipid vesicles in vitro (Kevany et al., 2013), and heterologously expressed PRPH2 generates high curvature membranes in cells (Milstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milstein et al., 2017.

claim: Many mutations leading to blindness are caused by distortions in ROS ultrastructure or completely abolish ROS formation.
source: While many mutations leading to blindness are caused by distortions in ROS ultrastructure, or completely abolish ROS formation (Boon et al., 2008; Daiger et al., 2013), the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unresolved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boon et al., 2008; Daiger et al., 2013.

claim: Mouse ROS were extracted using a fast retinal detachment method, minimizing structural deterioration.
source: Mouse ROS were extracted using a fast retinal detachment method, minimizing structural deterioration.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the sample preparation.

claim: A single mechanical disruption was employed to detach ROS from the retina at the junction of their thin connecting cilium.
source: We employed a single mechanical disruption to detach ROS from the retina at the junction of their thin connecting cilium (CC).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the sample preparation.

claim: Examination of extracted ROS by light microscopy revealed intact ROS with the expected length on the order of 20 µm.
source: Examination of extracted ROS by light microscopy revealed intact ROS with the expected length on the order of 20 µm (Nickell et al., 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by light microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and a citation to Nickell et al., 2007.

claim: Lamellae typically contained several ROS as revealed by TEM overview images.
source: Lamellae typically contained several ROS as revealed by TEM overview images (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by TEM overview images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Conventional tomograms acquired with defocus reveal the highly ordered ROS membrane architecture.
source: Conventional tomograms acquired with defocus reveal the highly ordered ROS membrane architecture (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by tomographic data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: The use of the Volta phase plate (VPP) enhanced the contrast and allowed for the direct observation of cytosolic protein densities.
source: The use of the Volta phase plate (VPP) (Danev et al., 2014) further enhanced the contrast and allowed for the direct observation of cytosolic protein densities (Figure 1B, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by tomographic data shown in Figure 1B, Videos 2 and 3, and a citation to Danev et al., 2014.

claim: Tomograms of ROS show that the supramolecular organization of the disk membranes exhibits the expected order over a range of micrometers.
source: Tomograms of ROS show that the supramolecular organization of the disk membranes exhibits the expected order over a range of micrometers.
evidence: This is based on the tomographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The resulting distances agree with previous studies of mammalian ROS.
source: The resulting distances (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 5) agree with previous studies of mammalian ROS (Nickell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C, D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and a citation to Nickell et al., 2007.

claim: The regular inter disk spacing is overall preserved across species.
source: The regular inter disk spacing is overall preserved across species (Nickell et al., 2007), and therefore defines with nanometer precision the 3D spatial framework within which fast molecular diffusion processes of phototransduction take place (Calvert et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nickell et al., 2007 and Calvert et al., 2001.

claim: The regular inter disk spacing defines with nanometer precision the 3D spatial framework within which fast molecular diffusion processes of phototransduction take place.
source: The regular inter disk spacing is overall preserved across species (Nickell et al., 2007), and therefore defines with nanometer precision the 3D spatial framework within which fast molecular diffusion processes of phototransduction take place (Calvert et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Calvert et al., 2001.

claim: Cryo-EM 2D projections show zipper-like patterns similar to those observed in metal-stained, plastic-embedded ROS sections.
source: It was previously suggested that the close proximity between disks is maintained by connectivity between the disk membranes, a model derived from 2D micrographs of metal-stained, plastic-embedded ROS sections showing zipper-like structures (Robertson, 1965). Cryo-EM 2D projections show similar patterns (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D projections shown in Figure 1E and F, and a citation to Robertson, 1965.

claim: At a different tilt angle, the zipper-like pattern is resolved into the disk incisure.
source: At a different tilt angle, however, the pattern is resolved into the disk incisure (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Tomographic reconstruction confirmed that the membranes at these positions are not interconnected.
source: Tomographic reconstruction confirmed that the membranes at these positions are not interconnected (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by tomographic data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The proposed model of continuous disk membranes is likely based on a misinterpretation of projection images that are disentangled by 3D imaging.
source: We therefore conclude that the proposed model of continuous disk membranes is likely based on a misinterpretation of projection images that are disentangled by 3D imaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tomographic data presented.

claim: Structures that connect membranes of two adjacent disks were observed in the raw and filtered tomograms acquired with the VPP.
source: In agreement with these previous findings, we observed structures that connect membranes of two adjacent disks in the raw (Figure 1B) and filtered (Figure 2A–C) tomograms acquired with the VPP, but they were not discernible in the conventional tomograms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by tomographic data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2A–C.

claim: Connectors were visualized in proximity to the disk rims, both at the outer periphery of the disks and at the disk incisures.
source: Connectors were visualized in proximity to the disk rims, both at the outer periphery of the disks (Figure 2A, Video 4) and at the disk incisures (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by tomographic data shown in Figure 2A, B, and Video 4.

claim: Densities that seem to connect the parallel membranes at the disk interior were found at lower frequency.
source: In addition, densities that seem to connect the parallel membranes at the disk interior were found at lower frequency (Figure 2C, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by tomographic data shown in Figure 2C and Video 5.

claim: Over 90% of the connectors were picked by both automated and manual segmentation methods.
source: Over 90% of the connectors were picked by both methods and the error of the determined coordinates was below 2 nm.
evidence: This is based on comparison of automated and manual segmentation methods.

claim: The error of the determined connector coordinates was below 2 nm.
source: Over 90% of the connectors were picked by both methods and the error of the determined coordinates was below 2 nm.
evidence: This is based on comparison of automated and manual segmentation methods.

claim: Automated segmentation was performed on five tomograms resulting in the segmentation of 7000 connectors.
source: Automated segmentation was performed on five tomograms resulting in the segmentation of 7000 connectors.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the data analysis.

claim: Rim connectors have shorter nearest-neighbor distances compared to disk interior connectors.
source: Statistical analysis showed that rim connectors have shorter nearest-neighbor distances (Figure 2E), are shorter (Figure 2F), and have a lower grey value; that is, represent a more dense structure (Figure 2G) compared to the disk interior connectors.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Rim connectors are shorter than disk interior connectors.
source: Statistical analysis showed that rim connectors have shorter nearest-neighbor distances (Figure 2E), are shorter (Figure 2F), and have a lower grey value; that is, represent a more dense structure (Figure 2G) compared to the disk interior connectors.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Rim connectors have a lower grey value, representing a more dense structure, compared to disk interior connectors.
source: Statistical analysis showed that rim connectors have shorter nearest-neighbor distances (Figure 2E), are shorter (Figure 2F), and have a lower grey value; that is, represent a more dense structure (Figure 2G) compared to the disk interior connectors.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The statistical analysis results implied the existence of two distinct types of connectors.
source: These results implied the existence of two distinct types of connectors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of connector properties.

claim: The density of the connectors is estimated to be 190 and 920 molecules per μm2 of the disk membrane surface area for the rim and interior connectors, respectively.
source: Based on the segmentation, we estimated the density of the connectors per surface area of disk to be 190 and 920 molecules per μm2 of the disk membrane surface area for the rim and interior connectors, respectively (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the segmentation data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Disk rim connectors are tentatively assigned to glutamic-acid-rich protein 2 (GARP2).
source: By integrating available experimental data (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Gilliam et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2019) and mass-spectrometry data (Kwok et al., 2008; Skiba et al., 2013), we tentatively assign disk rim connectors to glutamic-acid-rich protein 2 (GARP2), and the interior species to the enzyme phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6).
evidence: This is a tentative assignment based on integration of experimental and mass-spectrometry data from multiple sources.

claim: Disk interior connectors are tentatively assigned to the enzyme phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6).
source: By integrating available experimental data (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Gilliam et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2019) and mass-spectrometry data (Kwok et al., 2008; Skiba et al., 2013), we tentatively assign disk rim connectors to glutamic-acid-rich protein 2 (GARP2), and the interior species to the enzyme phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6).
evidence: This is a tentative assignment based on integration of experimental and mass-spectrometry data from multiple sources.

claim: The authors were not able to validate the tentative assignment of connectors experimentally.
source: However, we were not able to validate this assignment experimentally.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Due to the structural flexibility of the connectors, further structural information could not be obtained by alignment, classification, and averaging of connector subvolumes.
source: Due to the obvious structural flexibility of the connectors observed in the raw data (Figure 2A–C), we could not obtain further structural information by alignment, classification, and averaging of connector subvolumes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on the raw data shown in Figure 2A–C and the subvolume averaging results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The disk rims have a 12 nm radius of curvature.
source: The second key structural feature of ROS architecture is the high curvature at the disk rims. There, the two membrane bilayers of a disk are connected via a hairpin-like structure, with a 12 nm radius of curvature.
evidence: This is a measurement derived from the cryo-ET data.

claim: The disk rim subvolume average showed three densities inside the disk lumen.
source: The resulting average showed three densities (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Video 7) inside the disk lumen.
evidence: This is supported by the subvolume average shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Video 7.

claim: In 3D, the three densities form an ordered assembly of repeats organized in three interconnected rows, creating a continuous belt along the disk rim.
source: In 3D, they form an ordered assembly of repeats organized in three interconnected rows, creating a continuous belt along the disk rim (focused on the central row in Figure 3A, Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by the 3D subvolume average shown in Figure 3A and Video 8.

claim: A repeat length of 4.1 nm was measured for all three rows in the disk rim average.
source: We measured a repeat length of 4.1 nm for all three rows in this average and a shift of half a repeat between the central and peripheral rows (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: There is a shift of half a repeat between the central and peripheral rows.
source: We measured a repeat length of 4.1 nm for all three rows in this average and a shift of half a repeat between the central and peripheral rows (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The view from the disk lumen onto the assembly appears to be C2 symmetric with respect to an axis perpendicular to the ROS axis.
source: The view from the disk lumen onto the assembly appears to be C2 symmetric with respect to an axis perpendicular to the ROS axis.
evidence: This is an observation based on the subvolume average.

claim: The densities of the central row have a height of ~11 nm, stretching from the cytosol, through the membrane bilayer, and into the disk lumen.
source: The densities of the central row have a height of ~11 nm, stretching from the cytosol, through the membrane bilayer, and into the disk lumen (along the z-axis in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on measurements from the subvolume average shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Each repeat contributes two small cytosolic densities.
source: Each repeat contributes two small cytosolic densities.
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average.

claim: The cytosolic domain of the repeat is 1.0 nm.
source: This 1.0 nm cytosolic domain is followed by a transmembrane domain extending over 6.0 nm with two diverging densities.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the subvolume average.

claim: The transmembrane domain extends over 6.0 nm with two diverging densities.
source: This 1.0 nm cytosolic domain is followed by a transmembrane domain extending over 6.0 nm with two diverging densities.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the subvolume average.

claim: The two densities converge inside the disk lumen into a globular domain with a height of 2.6 nm.
source: These two densities then converge inside the disk lumen into a globular domain with a height of 2.6 nm.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the subvolume average.

claim: The densities within a repeat and its neighbors in the row come into close contact inside the disk lumen.
source: There, the densities within a repeat and its neighbors in the row come into close contact.
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average.

claim: Two diverging arms connect the central row to the peripheral rows.
source: Farther into the disk lumen, two diverging arms connect the central row to the peripheral rows.
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average.

claim: A repeat in the central row contacts two repeats, one on each of the peripheral rows located diagonally and inclined at an angle of ~63° with respect to the central repeat.
source: A repeat in the central row contacts two repeats, one on each of the peripheral rows located diagonally and inclined at an angle of ~63° with respect to the central repeat (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average and analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The head domain has a height of 1.5 nm.
source: The head domain has a height of 1.5 nm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on measurements from the subvolume average shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The shape and the dimensions of repeats in the peripheral rows are similar to the central row.
source: The shape and the dimensions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B, Video 9) of repeats in the peripheral rows are similar to the central row; however, a pronounced density connects the peripheral repeats along the outside of the assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, Video 10).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume averages shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B, C, and Videos 9 and 10.

claim: A pronounced density connects the peripheral repeats along the outside of the assembly.
source: The shape and the dimensions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B, Video 9) of repeats in the peripheral rows are similar to the central row; however, a pronounced density connects the peripheral repeats along the outside of the assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, Video 10).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and Video 10.

claim: The absence of ABCA4 has little impact on the architecture of the disk rim scaffold.
source: To clarify the identity of the scaffold proteins, we analyzed the disk rims in VPP datasets of WT mice (WTVPP) and of homozygote ABCA4 knockout mice (Abca4-/-VPP). The overall quality of the VPP averages is lower than for WTconv, but cross-sections through the disk rim averages filtered to the same resolution reveal a similar structure in all three cases (Figure 4). Hence, the absence of ABCA4 has little impact on the architecture of the disk rim scaffold.
evidence: This is based on comparison of disk rim averages from WT and ABCA4 knockout mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: The shape of the repeats is clearly different from the ABCA4 structure.
source: Furthermore, the shape of the repeats is clearly different from the ABCA4 structure (Liu et al., 2021; Tsybovsky and Palczewski, 2014) while it agrees with the previously estimated dimensions of PRPH2-ROM1 tetramers (Kevany et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published ABCA4 structures and PRPH2-ROM1 tetramer dimensions.

claim: The shape of the repeats agrees with the previously estimated dimensions of PRPH2-ROM1 tetramers.
source: Furthermore, the shape of the repeats is clearly different from the ABCA4 structure (Liu et al., 2021; Tsybovsky and Palczewski, 2014) while it agrees with the previously estimated dimensions of PRPH2-ROM1 tetramers (Kevany et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kevany et al., 2013.

claim: A model of PRPH2 dimers predicted by AlphaFold2 matches the V-shape and the size of the repeats.
source: However, a model of PRPH2 dimers predicted by AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021; Mirdita et al., 2021) matches the V-shape and the size of the repeats equally well (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Video 11).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the AlphaFold2 model with the subvolume average shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Video 11.

claim: The disk rim scaffold enforces the high membrane curvature at ROS disk rims and is composed of three interconnected rows of PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the disk rim scaffold enforces the high membrane curvature at ROS disk rims and is composed of three interconnected rows of PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the cryo-ET data and subvolume averaging results.

claim: A density map with near-atomic resolution would be needed to conclusively determine whether the repeats are PRPH2-ROM1 dimers or tetramers.
source: To test this hypothesis and to conclusively determine whether the repeats are PRPH2-ROM1 dimers or tetramers, a density map with near-atomic resolution would be needed.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study and future directions.

claim: The optimization of a ROS preparation method for cryo-ET that is gentler and faster than previously reported procedures enabled the advancement in understanding ROS organization.
source: This advancement was enabled by the optimization of a ROS preparation method for cryo-ET that is gentler and faster than previously reported procedures (Gilliam et al., 2012; Nickell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to previous procedures.

claim: Although some ROS were damaged during the preparation, areas with structurally well-preserved ROS were easily identified and used exclusively for imaging.
source: Although some ROS were damaged during the preparation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), areas with structurally well-preserved ROS were easily identified and used exclusively for imaging.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cryo-ET is a powerful tool to visualize the 3D molecular architectures of cells in a close-to-native state.
source: Cryo-ET is a powerful tool to visualize the 3D molecular architectures of cells in a close-to-native state (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a general statement about the cryo-ET method supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Tomograms acquired with VPP exhibited enhanced contrast, revealing the molecular landscape in ROS and enabling identification of connectors between ROS disk membranes.
source: Tomograms acquired with VPP exhibited enhanced contrast, revealing the molecular landscape in ROS and they enabled us to identify connectors between ROS disk membranes.
evidence: This is based on the VPP tomographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar connectors have been observed previously.
source: Similar connectors have been observed previously (Corless and Schneider, 1987; Nickell et al., 2007; Roof and Heuser, 1982; Usukura and Yamada, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The high quality of the data allowed quantitative assessment of connectors between disks by segmenting them with a modified Pyto workflow.
source: The high quality of our data allowed us to quantitatively assess these connectors between disks, by segmenting them with a modified Pyto workflow, and their statistical analysis confirmed the existence of two distinct connector species.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the data analysis.

claim: Statistical analysis confirmed the existence of two distinct connector species.
source: The high quality of our data allowed us to quantitatively assess these connectors between disks, by segmenting them with a modified Pyto workflow, and their statistical analysis confirmed the existence of two distinct connector species.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the segmented connectors.

claim: Disk rim connectors are shorter and more densely packed.
source: The disk rim connectors are shorter and more densely packed (Usukura and Yamada, 1981), while disk interior connectors are longer and fewer (Kajimura et al., 2000; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2 and citations to Usukura and Yamada, 1981.

claim: Disk interior connectors are longer and fewer.
source: The disk rim connectors are shorter and more densely packed (Usukura and Yamada, 1981), while disk interior connectors are longer and fewer (Kajimura et al., 2000; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2 and a citation to Kajimura et al., 2000.

claim: Disk rim connectors were reported previously in frog ROS as part of the 'terminal loop complex' which appeared to be arranged in a 2D lattice.
source: Disk rim connectors were reported previously in frog ROS as part of the 'terminal loop complex' which appeared to be arranged in a 2D lattice (Corless et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corless et al., 1987.

claim: The data suggest that the localization of disk rim connectors in mice is more variable because of their broad distribution of nearest-neighbor distances.
source: Our data suggest that the localization of disk rim connectors in mice is more variable because of their broad distribution of nearest-neighbor distances (Figure 2E) and the variable distances between disk rim connectors and the outer disk periphery (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 2E, 2A, and 2B.

claim: The CNGB1 gene encodes three partially disordered glutamic acid-rich proteins (GARPs): the β-subunit of the cyclic nucleotide gated cation channel (CNGC), and the alternatively-spliced proteins GARP1 and GARP2.
source: The CNGB1 gene encodes three partially disordered glutamic acid-rich proteins (GARPs) (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Colville and Molday, 1996); namely, the β-subunit of the cyclic nucleotide gated cation channel (CNGC), and the alternatively-spliced proteins GARP1 and GARP2.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Colville and Molday, 1996.

claim: All three GARPs are exclusively localized to disk rims or to the adjacent plasma membrane.
source: All three GARPs are exclusively localized to disk rims (Körschen et al., 1999) or to the adjacent PM.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Körschen et al., 1999.

claim: CNGCs mediate the cation conductance of the ROS plasma membrane in response to light.
source: CNGCs mediate the cation conductance of the ROS PM in response to light.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: GARP1 and GARP2 are soluble proteins which are tightly bound to membranes under physiological conditions by a hitherto unknown mechanism.
source: GARP1 and GARP2 are soluble proteins which are tightly bound to membranes under physiological conditions by a hitherto unknown mechanism (Körschen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Körschen et al., 1999.

claim: Loss of CNGCs has only a minor impact on ROS architecture.
source: While loss of CNGCs has only a minor impact on ROS architecture (Hüttl et al., 2005), knockout of all three GARP isoforms destabilizes the diameter of the disks and results in the misalignment of disk rims (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hüttl et al., 2005.

claim: Knockout of all three GARP isoforms destabilizes the diameter of the disks and results in the misalignment of disk rims.
source: While loss of CNGCs has only a minor impact on ROS architecture (Hüttl et al., 2005), knockout of all three GARP isoforms destabilizes the diameter of the disks and results in the misalignment of disk rims (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The finding that knockout of all three GARP isoforms destabilizes disk diameter and results in misalignment of disk rims suggests a structural role of either GARP1, GARP2 or both.
source: This finding suggests a structural role of either GARP1, GARP2 or both.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited knockout study.

claim: GARP1 is one order of magnitude less abundant in ROS than GARP2.
source: GARP1, however, is one order of magnitude less abundant in ROS than GARP2 (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) and cannot account for the estimated concentration of 190 disk rim connectors per μm2 disk.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006.

claim: GARP1 cannot account for the estimated concentration of 190 disk rim connectors per μm2 disk.
source: GARP1, however, is one order of magnitude less abundant in ROS than GARP2 (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) and cannot account for the estimated concentration of 190 disk rim connectors per μm2 disk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the abundance data and the measured connector density.

claim: GARP2 molecules form the connectors at the disk rim and organize the alignment of rims throughout the disk stack.
source: Thus, we suggest that GARP2 molecules form the connectors at the disk rim and organize the alignment of rims throughout the disk stack.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the abundance data and the measured connector density.

claim: GARP2 molecules likely form an oligomeric state.
source: It is likely that GARP2 molecules form an oligomeric state for the following reasons: (i) the hydrodynamic radius of GARP2 monomers is ~5 nm (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) and therefore too small to establish ~12 nm long connectors measured at high precision in our data (Figure 2F); (ii) GARP2 is known to be in equilibrium with dimeric and tetrameric species in vitro (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006); and (iii) we observe less disk rim connectors than expected, considering that GARP2 occurs with approximately 500 molecules per μm2 disk (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the hydrodynamic radius of GARP2 monomers, the measured connector length, and the known oligomeric states of GARP2.

claim: The hydrodynamic radius of GARP2 monomers is ~5 nm.
source: It is likely that GARP2 molecules form an oligomeric state for the following reasons: (i) the hydrodynamic radius of GARP2 monomers is ~5 nm (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) and therefore too small to establish ~12 nm long connectors measured at high precision in our data (Figure 2F); (ii) GARP2 is known to be in equilibrium with dimeric and tetrameric species in vitro (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006); and (iii) we observe less disk rim connectors than expected, considering that GARP2 occurs with approximately 500 molecules per μm2 disk (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006.

claim: GARP2 is known to be in equilibrium with dimeric and tetrameric species in vitro.
source: It is likely that GARP2 molecules form an oligomeric state for the following reasons: (i) the hydrodynamic radius of GARP2 monomers is ~5 nm (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) and therefore too small to establish ~12 nm long connectors measured at high precision in our data (Figure 2F); (ii) GARP2 is known to be in equilibrium with dimeric and tetrameric species in vitro (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006); and (iii) we observe less disk rim connectors than expected, considering that GARP2 occurs with approximately 500 molecules per μm2 disk (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006.

claim: GARP2 occurs with approximately 500 molecules per μm2 disk.
source: It is likely that GARP2 molecules form an oligomeric state for the following reasons: (i) the hydrodynamic radius of GARP2 monomers is ~5 nm (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) and therefore too small to establish ~12 nm long connectors measured at high precision in our data (Figure 2F); (ii) GARP2 is known to be in equilibrium with dimeric and tetrameric species in vitro (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006); and (iii) we observe less disk rim connectors than expected, considering that GARP2 occurs with approximately 500 molecules per μm2 disk (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Pugh and Lamb, 2000.

claim: Absence of all GARP isoforms does not abolish disk stacking.
source: Absence of all GARP isoforms does not abolish disk stacking (Gilliam et al., 2012), suggesting that the connectors in the disk interior can partially compensate for the loss of GARPs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gilliam et al., 2012.

claim: The connectors in the disk interior can partially compensate for the loss of GARPs.
source: Absence of all GARP isoforms does not abolish disk stacking (Gilliam et al., 2012), suggesting that the connectors in the disk interior can partially compensate for the loss of GARPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study.

claim: The most plausible candidate for the disk interior connectors is the enzyme phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6).
source: The most plausible candidate for these connectors is the enzyme phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the size and abundance of PDE6.

claim: The recently solved PDE6 structure shows that these 15 nm-long complex can bridge the 14 nm gap between adjacent disks.
source: The recently solved PDE6 structure (Gulati et al., 2019) shows that these 15 nm-long complex can bridge the 14 nm gap between adjacent disks and its abundance matches the results of our segmentation (Figure 2H; Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gulati et al., 2019 and the segmentation data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The abundance of PDE6 matches the results of the connector segmentation.
source: The recently solved PDE6 structure (Gulati et al., 2019) shows that these 15 nm-long complex can bridge the 14 nm gap between adjacent disks and its abundance matches the results of our segmentation (Figure 2H; Pugh and Lamb, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gulati et al., 2019; Pugh and Lamb, 2000 and the segmentation data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No other ROS protein exhibits the size and abundance required to contribute to the connectors visualized in the data.
source: To our knowledge, no other ROS protein exhibits the size and abundance required to contribute to the connectors visualized in our data (Kwok et al., 2008; Skiba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on mass-spectrometry data from Kwok et al., 2008; Skiba et al., 2013.

claim: GARP2 was previously proposed to form connectors between rims of disks by directly interacting with PRPH2.
source: GARP2 was previously proposed to form connectors between rims of disks (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006) by directly interacting with PRPH2 (Poetsch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Poetsch et al., 2001.

claim: The authors see no direct contact between the disk rim scaffold and disk rim connectors.
source: In contrast, we see no direct contact between the disk rim scaffold, which is likely composed of PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers, and disk rim connectors (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, C).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume averages shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, C.

claim: The subvolume average of disk rim connectors reveals no ordered transmembrane component linking the disk rim scaffold and connectors.
source: Furthermore, our subvolume average of disk rim connectors reveals no ordered transmembrane component linking the two structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C) as suggested previously (Corless et al., 1987).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C and a citation to Corless et al., 1987.

claim: The quality of the disk rim connector averages is limited by the low number of a few hundred available subvolumes.
source: However, the quality of our averages is limited by the low number of a few hundred available subvolumes.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the subvolume averaging.

claim: The mechanism by which disk rim connectors bind to the membrane and what determines their contact site remain to be elucidated.
source: The mechanism by which disk rim connectors bind to the membrane and what determines their contact site remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study and future directions.

claim: The authors could not observe connectors between disk rims and the plasma membrane in their tomograms as reported previously.
source: We could not observe connectors between disk rims and the plasma membrane in our tomograms as reported previously (Nickell et al., 2007; Roof and Heuser, 1982).
evidence: This is based on the tomographic data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Connectors between disk rims and the plasma membrane were suggested to be formed by the GARP-part of the CNGC β-subunit.
source: These connectors were suggested to be formed by the GARP-part of the CNGC β-subunit (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Poetsch et al., 2001), interacting with PRPH2 in disk rims (Pearring et al., 2021; Poetsch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Poetsch et al., 2001; Pearring et al., 2021.

claim: It is possible that the density of the intrinsically disordered GARP-part is not resolved as a clear connector in the tomograms.
source: It is possible that the density of the intrinsically disordered GARP-part is not resolved as a clear connector in our tomograms.
evidence: This is a speculation about why the connectors were not observed.

claim: Connectors between disk rims and the plasma membrane would be expected to be present in only a few copies within the small field-of-view of the tomograms.
source: Furthermore, they would be expected to be present in only a few copies within the small field-of-view of our tomograms.
evidence: This is a speculation about why the connectors were not observed.

claim: While proteins for the experiments leading to the model were purified from mammalian sources, the model assumes a distance of 10 nm between the PM and disk rims.
source: Interestingly, while proteins for the experiments leading to the model were purified from mammalian sources (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Poetsch et al., 2001), the model assumes a distance of 10 nm between the PM and disk rims (Batra-Safferling et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on citations to Batra-Safferling et al., 2006; Poetsch et al., 2001.

claim: The distance of 10 nm between the PM and disk rims assumed in the model was derived from amphibians and deviates considerably from recent results in mice (~25 nm).
source: This value was derived from amphibians (Roof and Heuser, 1982) and deviates considerably from recent results 18 nm, (Gilliam et al., 2012) and from our current measurements in mice (~25 nm).
evidence: This is based on citations to Roof and Heuser, 1982; Gilliam et al., 2012 and the measurements in the current study.

claim: The structural analysis of the ROS disk rim allowed resolution of the crescentic rim density as part of the 'terminal loop complex' into a continuous protein scaffold for the first time.
source: Our structural analysis of the ROS disk rim allowed us to resolve for the first time the crescentic rim density as part of the 'terminal loop complex' (Corless et al., 1987) into a continuous protein scaffold.
evidence: This is based on the subvolume averaging results and a citation to Corless et al., 1987.

claim: Only three proteins exist in ROS which are abundant, localized to the disk rim, and contain large disk luminal domains: PRPH2, ROM1, and ABCA4.
source: To our knowledge, only three proteins exist in ROS which are abundant, localized to the disk rim, and contain large disk luminal domains; namely, the homologs PRPH2 (Molday et al., 1987) and ROM1 (Bascom et al., 1992) which form noncovalent homo- and hetero-oligomers (Goldberg and Molday, 1996), and ABCA4 (Papermaster et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Molday et al., 1987; Bascom et al., 1992; Goldberg and Molday, 1996; Papermaster et al., 1978.

claim: Given the compact and ordered structure of the scaffold, ABCA4 is likely not a component of it.
source: Absence of ABCA4 does not significantly alter the structure of the disk rim scaffold (Figure 4), and we therefore suggest that given the compact and ordered structure of the scaffold, ABCA4 is likely not a component of it (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on the comparison of disk rim averages from WT and ABCA4 knockout mice shown in Figure 4 and the model shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The luminal domain of ABCA4 is too large to be accommodated in the disk interior.
source: The luminal domain of ABCA4 is too large to be accommodated in the disk interior (Liu et al., 2021; Tsybovsky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2021; Tsybovsky et al., 2013.

claim: ABCA4 likely resides next to the scaffold at the disk rim.
source: Hence, we propose ABCA4 resides next to the scaffold at the disk rim.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and the size of ABCA4.

claim: Whether ABCA4 interacts with the rim scaffold or locates at a distance from it remains unclear.
source: However, whether ABCA4 interacts with the rim scaffold or locates at a distance from it remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: An AlphaFold2 model predicted for the PRPH2 dimer closely resembles the V-shape and the size of the repeats observed in the disk rim average at a resolution of 18 Å.
source: Recently, AlphaFold2 has proven its ability to predict the 3D structure of not only monomeric proteins with high accuracy (Jumper et al., 2021) but also that of small oligomeric complexes (Evans et al., 2021; Mirdita et al., 2021). An AlphaFold2 model predicted for the PRPH2 dimer closely resembles the V-shape and the size of the repeats observed in our disk rim average at a resolution of 18 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Video 11).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 model and the disk rim average shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Video 11, and citations to Jumper et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Mirdita et al., 2021.

claim: The previously published low-resolution negative stain structure of PRPH2-ROM1 complexes interpreted as tetramers has approximately the same size as the predicted dimer structure.
source: The previously published low-resolution negative stain structure of PRPH2-ROM1 complexes interpreted as tetramers (Kevany et al., 2013) has approximately the same size as the predicted dimer structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the published structure and a citation to Kevany et al., 2013.

claim: At the current resolution, the disk rim scaffold appears to be C2 symmetric.
source: At the current resolution, the disk rim scaffold appears to be C2 symmetric (Figures 3A and 5A), which is compatible with the predicted model of PRPH2 dimers (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and the C2 symmetry axis found for the negative stain structure of putative PRPH2-ROM1 tetramers (Kevany et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume averages shown in Figures 3A and 5A, the AlphaFold2 model shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and a citation to Kevany et al., 2013.

claim: Non-covalently bound PRPH2-ROM1 complexes form higher order oligomers stabilized by disulfide bonds, which are essential for normal disk morphogenesis.
source: Non-covalently bound PRPH2-ROM1 complexes are known to form higher order oligomers stabilized by disulfide bonds (Loewen and Molday, 2000), which are essential for normal disk morphogenesis (Milstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Loewen and Molday, 2000; Milstein et al., 2020.

claim: The intermolecular disulfide bridges are exclusively formed by the PRPH2-C150 and ROM1-C153 cysteine residues which are located in the luminal domain.
source: The intermolecular disulfide brides are exclusively formed by the PRPH2-C150 and ROM1-C153 cysteine residues which are located in the luminal domain (Zulliger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zulliger et al., 2018.

claim: The authors hypothesize that the disulfide bonds are responsible for the contacts across rows or between repeats of the peripheral rows.
source: We hypothesize that these disulfide bonds (Figure 5B), are responsible for the contacts across rows (Figure 3) or between repeats of the peripheral rows (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the subvolume averages shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, and the model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Docking the predicted model of the PRPH2 dimer into the repeats of the central row reveals that the two PRPH-C150 cysteine residues are not located where the contacts are observed but closer toward the inner membrane leaflet.
source: Docking the predicted model of the PRPH2 dimer into the repeats of the central row, however, reveals that the two PRPH-C150 cysteine residues are not located where we observe these contacts but closer toward the inner membrane leaflet (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B, Video 11).
evidence: This is based on the docked model shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and Video 11.

claim: The discrepancy in the location of PRPH-C150 cysteine residues may be explained by errors in the prediction or the dimers assuming a different conformation upon oligomerization and embedding into the highly curved membrane environment of the disk rim.
source: This may be explained by errors in the prediction or the dimers assuming a different conformation upon oligomerization and embedding into the highly curved membrane environment of the disk rim.
evidence: This is a speculation about the discrepancy.

claim: PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers isolated from native sources exhibit varying degrees of polymerization.
source: PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers isolated from native sources exhibit varying degrees of polymerization (Loewen and Molday, 2000) and ROM1 is excluded from larger PRPH2 oligomers (Milstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Loewen and Molday, 2000; Milstein et al., 2020.

claim: ROM1 is excluded from larger PRPH2 oligomers.
source: PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers isolated from native sources exhibit varying degrees of polymerization (Loewen and Molday, 2000) and ROM1 is excluded from larger PRPH2 oligomers (Milstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milstein et al., 2020.

claim: The authors could not resolve the heterogeneity of PRPH2-ROM1 oligomers as additional structures to sufficient quality by subvolume averaging.
source: We could not resolve this heterogeneity as additional structures to sufficient quality by subvolume averaging, but in combination with the inherent flexibility of the disk rim, it might be the reason for the restricted resolution of our averages.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the subvolume averaging.

claim: The heterogeneity and inherent flexibility of the disk rim might be the reason for the restricted resolution of the averages.
source: We could not resolve this heterogeneity as additional structures to sufficient quality by subvolume averaging, but in combination with the inherent flexibility of the disk rim, it might be the reason for the restricted resolution of our averages.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for the limited resolution.

claim: A model involving V-shaped PRPH2-ROM1 tetramers for membrane curvature formation was proposed recently.
source: A model involving V-shaped PRPH2-ROM1 tetramers for membrane curvature formation was proposed recently (Milstein et al., 2020), but it comprises two rows of tetramers as basic building block of the disk rim scaffold which are linked in a head-to-head manner.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milstein et al., 2020.

claim: The analysis in situ resolves three rows of repeats which are linked by the luminal domain but are rather organized side-by-side.
source: Instead, our analysis in situ resolves three rows of repeats which are also linked by the luminal domain but are rather organized side-by-side (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average and the model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The results raise the question whether the basic building blocks of the disk rim scaffold are PRPH2-ROM1 dimers or tetramers.
source: Furthermore, our results raise the question whether the basic building blocks of the disk rim scaffold are PRPH2-ROM1 dimers or tetramers.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the results.

claim: The authors propose a mechanism for disk rim curvature formation, where the two diverging transmembrane densities of V-shaped PRPH2-ROM1 complexes displace lipids in the inner membrane leaflet.
source: We propose a mechanism for disk rim curvature formation, where the two diverging transmembrane densities of V-shaped PRPH2-ROM1 complexes displace lipids in the inner membrane leaflet.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the subvolume average.

claim: While unlinked PRPH2-ROM1 complexes are able to induce some membrane curvature, their oligomerization into three continuous rows is required to force the membrane into the elongated, highly curved geometry.
source: While unlinked complexes are able to induce some membrane curvature, their oligomerization into three continuous rows is required to force the membrane into this elongated, highly curved geometry (Milstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milstein et al., 2020 and the subvolume average.

claim: The data indicate that the luminal domains of complexes hold the disk rim scaffold together.
source: Our data indicate that the luminal domains of complexes hold the disk rim scaffold together (Figure 3C), which is consistent with the fact that most pathological mutations of PRPH2 affect its luminal domain (Boon et al., 2008; Goldberg et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on the subvolume average shown in Figure 3C and citations to Boon et al., 2008; Goldberg et al., 2001.

claim: Most pathological mutations of PRPH2 affect its luminal domain.
source: Our data indicate that the luminal domains of complexes hold the disk rim scaffold together (Figure 3C), which is consistent with the fact that most pathological mutations of PRPH2 affect its luminal domain (Boon et al., 2008; Goldberg et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boon et al., 2008; Goldberg et al., 2001.

claim: It is possible that pathological mutations of PRPH2 impair the formation of complexes and their disulfide bond-stabilized oligomerization.
source: In good agreement with previous work, it is possible that these mutations impair the formation of complexes and their disulfide bond-stabilized oligomerization (Chang et al., 2002; Conley et al., 2019; Zulliger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2002; Conley et al., 2019; Zulliger et al., 2018.

claim: Alterations in PRPH2 could impede or completely prevent disk morphogenesis which would disrupt the structural integrity of ROS, compromise the viability of the retina and ultimately lead to blindness.
source: Hence, these alterations could impede or completely prevent disk morphogenesis which, in turn, would disrupt the structural integrity of ROS, compromise the viability of the retina and ultimately lead to blindness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed mechanism and the known effects of PRPH2 mutations.

claim: Five- to 8-week-old wild type (WT) mice (C57BL/6 J, Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, USA) and mice lacking the photoreceptor-specific ATP binding cassette transporter ABCA4 (Abca4-/-) were used for the isolation of rod outer segments (ROS).
source: Five- to 8-week-old wild type (WT) mice (C57BL/6 J, Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, USA) and mice lacking the photoreceptor-specific ATP binding cassette transporter ABCA4 (Abca4-/-) (Weng et al., 1999), were used for the isolation of rod outer segments (ROS).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the mouse strains used.

claim: The Cryo-ET data provide novel quantitative and structural information on the molecular architecture in ROS.
source: Our Cryo-ET data provide novel quantitative and structural information on the molecular architecture in ROS and substantiate previous results on proposed mechanisms underlying pathologies of certain PRPH2 mutations leading to blindness.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contributions of the study.

claim: The Cryo-ET data substantiate previous results on proposed mechanisms underlying pathologies of certain PRPH2 mutations leading to blindness.
source: Our Cryo-ET data provide novel quantitative and structural information on the molecular architecture in ROS and substantiate previous results on proposed mechanisms underlying pathologies of certain PRPH2 mutations leading to blindness.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contributions of the study.
